items.title: Myra Menville Interview, 1958-05-07, 09
items.q: Now, Robichaud, who was this left-hand... Both Negro bands, light Negro, was a left-hand violinist, and he had a society orchestra too.

ctx.x: A form of jazz music that you were playing? It was definitely not ragtime, I can tell you that. It was my interpretation of the difference between jazz and ragtime is, if you'll put it as simply as possible, is one is jerkier than the other one. And let's say the same difference that there is between jazz and swing, there is between ragtime and jazz. It was a smoother type of the same sort of music. But then our interest in the music became very deeper, much deeper personally, not with any idea of analysis. I…
Well, let's get back to the social aspect of it for the world in society. When you first started going to parties, they tend to have Negro bands or jazz bands or white or colored.

items.title: Edmond "Doc" Souchon Interview, 1962-02-17
items.q: Now, Robichaud, to me, he was one of the most polished gentlemen that I ever knew.

ctx.x: And you mentioned the other day you'd like to tell us something about that.

Now, Robichaud, to me, he was one of the most polished gentlemen that I ever knew. He was soft-spoken, very well educated, and as we all know, he was a left-hand violinist. And strictly readers, every one of them in the band, they had their arrangements up in front of them. But he always had one or two hot takeoff men in the band. He may have a nucleus of six, but he'd have either a good trumpet or a good takeoff clarinet. I'm very certain that I've often heard Perez play in that group there. Once in a while,…
What type of music otherwise, I mean, in the way of waltzes or...
